managers.name: Kaden Smith
managers.bio:
Kaden Smith is the closest thing this league has to a dynasty. #1 all-time Power Score, the best career win percentage in league history (.628), the most career points scored, and the only manager with two championship game appearances (2023, 2025) — the resume speaks for itself. The 2023 title was as dominant as it gets: best regular season record, #1 seed, wire-to-wire champion, no real drama.

But the record isn't spotless, and that's what makes Kaden interesting. 2024 was a genuine stumble — 6-8, 9th place, a rare down year sandwiched between two excellent ones — and Chase Potter, Kaden's own division rival, actually owns the head-to-head 2-1 despite Kaden's overall dominance. Josh Allen has been the QB1 for 43 straight weeks, the longest player-team tenure in league history, which says a lot about a manager who builds around a core and doesn't panic-trade it away.

Player type: the empire builder. Elite floor, championship pedigree, and the numbers to back up the reputation — but not invincible, and the manager everyone else in the league is chasing.

managers.name: Jeffrey Taylor
managers.bio:
Jeffrey Taylor has quietly built one of the best regular-season resumes in the league — a 26-17 career record, the 2nd-best win percentage in league history (.605) — without a single championship to show for it. One runner-up finish (2023) is the extent of the hardware, and the bracket record (1-2) hasn't matched the regular-season one.

2025 was the outlier: a 5-9 finish, easily the worst season on record, dropping Jeffrey from perennial contender territory. On the bright side, Jeffrey owns the closest margin of victory in league history — a 0.1-point nail-biter in 2024 — proof that when the games are tight, this is a manager who finds a way to be on the right side of them, most of the time.

Player type: the perpetual contender without a ring. Consistently good, rarely great when it counts most, and 2025 raises the question of whether the window is closing.

managers.name: Chase Potter
managers.bio:
Chase Potter is a study in extremes. The 2024 championship run was as clean as it gets — a perfect 3-0 bracket as the #3 seed — and Chase also owns the single most lopsided win in league history, a 146.46-point demolition of Tyson Garff in the 2024 semifinals. When this team peaks, nobody in the league is better.

The problem is consistency. 2025 fell off a cliff — 6-8, a finish that dropped from 1st place the year before all the way to 9th — and Chase is also the most active manager in the transaction log, 116 career moves, well above the league median. That's a lot of tinkering for a team that's finished anywhere from 1st to 10th in three seasons.

Player type: the high-variance tinkerer. Capable of the best week anyone's ever had, but the aggressive roster management cuts both ways — boom seasons and bust seasons, rarely anything in between.

managers.name: Brandon Evans
managers.bio:
Brandon Evans is the definition of steady — a 24-19 career record, tied for the 3rd-best win percentage in the league (.558), and the distinction of never once finishing in last place across three seasons. The 2024 3rd-place finish is the high-water mark so far, backed by a career that's never had a real collapse.

What's missing is the signature moment. Zero championship appearances despite a win percentage that rivals actual champions — Brandon has quietly been one of the more reliable managers in the league without ever getting the credit that comes with hardware. The one place this team does show some teeth: a commanding 5-2 all-time record against division rival Jeffrey Taylor.

Player type: the steady hand. Never the story of the season, rarely the disaster either — the kind of manager whose consistency is easy to overlook until you actually look at the numbers.

managers.name: Tyson Garff
managers.bio:
Tyson Garff's regular-season numbers look like a contender's: a 24-19 career record, tied for the 3rd-best win percentage in the league. The problem shows up the moment the games matter most — 0-2 in the bracket across two playoff trips, with a best finish of 5th. The regular season has never once translated into a real postseason run.

Tyson is also the most active mover in the league not named Carston Christensen — 122 career transactions, constantly working the wire — and division rival Sam Trusty has been a persistent thorn, holding a 4-1 head-to-head edge. There's clearly a competitive manager in here; the results just haven't lined up with the effort in the moments that count.

Player type: the frustrated grinder. Works the roster as hard as anyone in the league, keeps the record respectable, and still hasn't broken through when the playoffs actually start.

managers.name: Garrett Larson
managers.bio:
Garrett Larson's three seasons look like three different managers ran the team. 2023: a solid 9-6, 4th place. 2024: an outright collapse, 3-11, dead last. 2025: a total reversal, 10-4, the league's best regular season and a trip to the 3rd-place game. Garrett is the only manager in league history to have posted both a best-regular-season-record finish AND a last-place finish — the definition of high-variance, year to year.

Division rival Rollin Rockett has taken the brunt of it lately, down 1-3 in the head-to-head, and the 2025 bounce-back suggests the 2024 disaster was more bad luck than bad management — a 22-21 career record with a strong 10-6 divisional mark backs that up.

Player type: the boom-bust roller coaster. Nobody in the league has a wider gap between their best and worst season — which makes Garrett either next year's champion or next year's cautionary tale, and there's no obvious way to know which until the games are played.

managers.name: Carston Christensen
managers.bio:
Carston Christensen is the league's most active roster manager by a wide margin — 169 career transactions, nearly 40% more than the next-closest manager — and the results have landed squarely in the middle every single time. Never finished better than 5th, never finished worse than 9th, across all three seasons. That's remarkable consistency for a manager who's constantly rebuilding the roster.

There's an irony that's hard to ignore: Carston literally named the 2025 team "2025 league champion" and finished 8th that year. The all-time divisional record (8-9) tracks with the overall profile — competent, active, but never quite building the roster that breaks into the top tier.

Player type: the overmanager. The most transactions, the least variance in outcome — proof that activity on the waiver wire doesn't automatically translate into wins, but also that it's kept this team from ever truly bottoming out.

managers.name: Gavin Chowen
managers.bio:
Gavin Chowen owns two of the most extreme entries in the record book, back to back. 2024: a 12-2 regular season, the best in league history, powered by a 10-game winning streak that's also the longest ever recorded. 2025: 5-9 and last place — the very next season. No one else in the league has gone from the best regular season on record to dead last in a single offseason.

The 2024 run did end in heartbreak — a runner-up finish after being the #1 seed — and the head-to-head with rival Britton Anderson has been close but unfavorable (2-3). The whole career (20-23, .465) reads almost exactly average, which undersells just how wild the actual path there has been.

Player type: the streak merchant. When this team gets hot, it gets hotter than anyone else in the league — the challenge has been what happens the year after the peak.

managers.name: Oliver Iverson
managers.bio:
Oliver Iverson's trajectory is the clearest improvement arc in the league: 13th place in 2023, up to 8th in 2024, up again to 6th and a playoff berth in 2025. No titles, no top-3 finishes yet, but the direction has been consistently up for three straight years — which is more than most managers in this league can claim.

It hasn't been painless getting here — a 9-game losing streak early in the 2023 season is tied for the longest in league history — which makes the climb back to a playoff spot two years later more impressive, not less. The head-to-head with division rival Carston Christensen sits at 2-3, a rivalry still finding its shape.

Player type: the developing prospect. Started at the bottom of the league, and has taken a real step forward every single season since — worth watching to see if 2026 is the year the patience pays off.

managers.name: Sam Trusty
managers.bio:
Sam Trusty is the league's proof that fantasy football has no memory, only nerve. Nobody else in the Gridiron Gentlemen's Society has swung this hard between disaster and triumph: a 2-12 regular season in 2024 — the worst any manager has ever posted, punctuated by a franchise-record 9-game losing streak that ran from Week 8 straight through Week 16 — and then, the very next year, an 8-6 finish and the 2025 championship. No one else in league history has gone from the bottom of the standings to the trophy in a single offseason.

That whiplash is basically the whole profile. Sam's career regular-season numbers are middling by design — a 19-24 record, a losing 105.9-to-113.1 career points for/against split — the résumé of a manager who treats 14 regular-season games as a formality. But hand Sam a bracket and the story flips completely: a league-best 4-1 all-time playoff record and two championship game appearances (2023, 2025) out of just two trips to the postseason. When it's win-or-go-home, Sam is the manager you least want across from you.

The Steelers fandom tracks. This is a manager who doesn't panic when things look bad on paper, grinds through the bad stretches (see: 2024), and shows up with something extra when the games start mattering. Division II rival Tyson Garff can attest — Sam owns that head-to-head 4-1. Playstyle-wise, think boom-or-bust roster management paired with ice in the veins come playoff time: not the most consistent manager week to week, but by far the most dangerous once October gives way to bracket play.

managers.name: Rollin Rockett
managers.bio:
Rollin Rockett spent two full seasons on the outside looking in — 13th in 2023, 10th in 2024 — before finally breaking through in 2025 with a playoff berth and a bracket win, both firsts in this manager's history. The career record (17-26, .395) is still one of the league's rougher ones, but the 2025 turn is a real signal, not just a fluke week.

Division rival Garrett Larson has been the bigger obstacle so far, holding a 3-1 head-to-head edge, and the road to respectability has clearly gone through some tough stretches. Still, first playoff trip, first playoff win, same season — that's meaningful progress.

Player type: the late bloomer. Two quiet years building toward something, and 2025 looked like the payoff — the real test is whether it's a new baseline or a one-year spike.

managers.name: Britton Anderson
managers.bio:
Britton Anderson holds a distinction nobody else in the league can claim: zero playoff appearances across all three seasons on record. A .395 career win percentage, tied for the worst in the league, and a roster that's never finished better than 7th. The numbers are the numbers here — this has been a rebuilding project since day one.

There's one genuine bright spot: a 3-2 all-time edge in the head-to-head with rival Gavin Chowen, proof that the results aren't uniformly bad, just insufficient to climb out of the bottom tier of the standings. The 2024 season (3-11) was the low point of an already difficult stretch.

Player type: still finding it. Every league needs a team working its way up from the bottom, and right now that's Britton — the head-to-head win over a divisional rival suggests the pieces for a turnaround aren't as far off as the standings make it look.
